name: Gastric sleeve

lead: Sleeve gastrectomy removes most of the stomach, leaving a narrow tube. It is a medical treatment for severe obesity and, according to Wikipedia, the most commonly performed bariatric operation worldwide. The appearance payoff people link to it is large fat loss, giving a leaner body and slimmer face.

Removing roughly three quarters or more of the stomach limits how much food can be eaten and removes the part that produces the appetite hormone ghrelin. Research also describes effects on gut hormones and glucose handling beyond weight loss alone. Systematic reviews report weight loss and resolution of conditions like type 2 diabetes comparable to gastric bypass. It is studied as a medical treatment, not a cosmetic one, and no studies on appearance outcomes were identified.

paras: It is usually done laparoscopically under general anaesthesia, with eligibility set by clinical guidelines based on body mass index and health conditions. Afterwards people follow staged diets and vitamin supplementation, and weight loss builds over many months.

Documented risks include staple-line leaks, bleeding, clots, infection, reflux, nausea and vomiting, vitamin and thiamine deficiencies (including rare Wernicke encephalopathy), gastric dilation, and weight regain that may lead to revision surgery. The operation is considered irreversible.

social.title: Ask HN: Hack my weight with a sleeve gastrectomy?

angle.text: A reduced stomach leads to large, sustained weight loss, which users link to a leaner body and slimmer face. It is studied for weight loss and diabetes in severe obesity, with documented surgical and nutritional risks.

lead: Sleeve gastrectomy, often called the gastric sleeve, is a bariatric operation usually performed laparoscopically in which a large portion of the stomach is removed along its greater curvature, leaving a narrow tube-shaped stomach. [1] It is used to treat severe obesity and obesity-related conditions such as type 2 diabetes. [2][3]

Wikipedia describes it as having begun as a modification of the duodenal switch and as the first stage of a two-step operation in very high-risk patients before being used on its own, and as now the most commonly performed bariatric surgery worldwide. [1] Systematic reviews report weight loss and comorbidity resolution comparable to gastric bypass, along with risks such as staple-line leak. [4][5]

The sources reviewed here concern the sleeve as a medical obesity treatment rather than a cosmetic one; its weight loss can change body and facial appearance, but no studies on appearance outcomes specifically were identified.
infobox: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, adjustable gastric band, duodenal switch
Leak, reflux, nutritional deficiency, weight regain

paras: The surgeon removes much of the stomach, which Wikipedia describes as leaving a remaining stomach of roughly 150 mL shaped over a calibration tube (bougie). [1] A first-in-human trial tested a fluorescence-guided calibration tube during sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass. [6] Variants include banded sleeve gastrectomy, which places a band to limit dilation of the sleeve. [7]

A 2014 JAMA systematic review of long-term follow-up after bariatric surgery assessed weight loss and the course of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia in severely obese adults and noted the limited number of long-term studies with good retention. [4]

Wikipedia reports typical excess-weight loss of 50-70% over two years and cites a 2021 Lancet meta-analysis linking bariatric surgery to lower all-cause mortality. [1] Studies in non-morbidly obese patients with diabetes have examined effects on insulin secretion. [8] A 2022 meta-analysis found better weight loss at 3 and 5 years after banded versus non-banded sleeve gastrectomy with no difference in comorbidity outcomes. [7]
Reviews note that the metabolic effects of bariatric surgery appear to exceed what weight loss alone would explain, and that changes to gastric emptying alter glucose handling. [9][10]

Large trials have compared the operation with others: a registered trial of sleeve gastrectomy versus gastric bypass enrolled 280 patients, one comparing gastric bypass, band and sleeve enrolled 1,351, and the BEST trial enrolled 1,752. [11][12][13] A trial in older patients compared sleeve and bypass. [14] Smaller randomized trials have examined analgesia after sleeve surgery, day-case discharge, omentopexy and gastric dilation, and anesthetic reversal. [15][16][17][18]

Observational work includes a review of gastric dilation after sleeve gastrectomy as a sole operation and a study of liraglutide for insufficient weight loss or regain after bariatric surgery. [19][20]

A systematic analysis of 4,888 patients examined staple-line leak, described as an ongoing concern, and a World Journal of Gastroenterology review covers its prevention and management. [5][21] Wikipedia lists leak, clots, infection, strictures, reflux, nausea, vitamin B12 deficiency, reduced bone health and weight regain among complications. [1]

A review of 118 cases described Wernicke encephalopathy after bariatric surgery, including after sleeve procedures, and advised testing and treating thiamine deficiency. [22] Case reports describe gastric twist obstruction after laparoscopic sleeve. [23] Studies have also looked at micronutrient status after the sleeve. [24]
